## Zigzag inclusions

In

$$
K_0\longrightarrow K_1\longleftarrow K_2,
$$

the left arrow means $K_0\subseteq K_1$ and the right-hand displayed arrow
means $K_2\subseteq K_1$. A backward arrow is not an inverse; it is an
inclusion whose direction is drawn towards the larger complex.

:::: {.worked-example}
### A transient loop

Let $K_0$ be the path $v_0-v_1-v_2$. Let $K_1$ add edge
$[v_2,v_0]$, producing a triangular outline, and let $K_2$ again be the path.
Both paths include into the outline:

$$
K_0\longrightarrow K_1\longleftarrow K_2.
$$

The first homology is zero, one-dimensional, then zero. The zigzag interval is
supported only at the middle index, and the arrows state how that event is
connected.
::::

When snapshots do not include directly, a union zigzag is one possible bridge:

$$
K_0\to K_0\cup K_1\leftarrow K_1
\to K_1\cup K_2\leftarrow K_2.
$$

The union is not neutral. It claims that both snapshots embed into a meaningful
common representation.

## Vineyard updates on a fixed complex

Let $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$ vary continuously on one fixed complex. At each time,
the sublevel filtration is

$$
K_{t,a}=\{\sigma\in K:f_t(\sigma)\leq a\}.
$$

Most small time steps preserve the ordering of simplices. A critical event
occurs when neighbouring simplices exchange filtration order. Vineyard
algorithms update the reduced boundary matrix through each adjacent
transposition and join the resulting birth-death positions into vine
segments. This differs from bottleneck matching, which compares completed
diagrams without using a path between their filtrations.

The Dionysus vineyard implementation exposes these updates for controlled
filtration homotopies; its official
[vineyard tutorial](https://mrzv.org/software/dionysus2/tutorial/vineyards.html)
shows the software-level calculation. The algorithm produces vines and
updated pairings, not every possible linear transport map between persistence
modules.

## Vineyard versus vineyard module

A vineyard records trajectories of persistence points. A vineyard module
additionally retains compatible maps between the persistence modules at
different external times. Schematically,

$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
V_s(a)&\longrightarrow&V_s(b)&\longrightarrow&V_s(c)\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
V_t(a+\eta)&\longrightarrow&V_t(b+\eta)&\longrightarrow&V_t(c+\eta).
\end{array}
$$

Horizontal arrows change filtration scale. Vertical arrows transport or
compare homology through external time. Each square should commute: changing
scale and then transporting must agree with transporting and then changing
scale. The [diagram-reading algebra refresher](../topic-02/algebra-survival-guide.qmd#reading-map-diagrams)
explains this notation.

![A vineyard follows diagram points, while a vineyard module additionally records linear maps between homology spaces.](../../assets/topic08-vineyard-versus-module.svg){fig-alt="The upper lane joins persistence points through time; the lower lane links vector spaces by linear maps."}

Source and target barcodes do not determine a particular map between their
modules. That missing linear information can matter for dynamic questions.

:::: {.worked-example}
### Why two visible vines need not separate algebraically

Turner's teaching example assigns four changing filtration values
[@turner2023vineyard]:

$$
f_t(A)=21-t,\quad f_t(B)=14-t,\quad
f_t(C)=15+t,\quad f_t(D)=t.
$$

At each time there are two visible intervals,

$$
[14-t,21-t),\qquad[t,15+t).
$$

Their endpoints trace two vines. Yet a coherent basis change can mix their
homology generators. Over $\mathbb F_2$, the relation

$$
[D]=[D+B]+[B]
$$

produces an off-diagonal transport term. The visible vineyard therefore does
not contain all of the module-level information. The example is important for
this distinction; its full representation-theoretic development is not
required for using snapshot persistence or ordinary vineyards.
::::

## Delicate cases

Smooth motion of points need not yield a gently changing Rips ordering. Many
edge lengths can cross together, changing triangles and higher-dimensional
simplices. Diagram stability bounds diagram displacement, but does not supply
reliable class identity:

$$
\text{diagram stability}\ne\text{feature tracking}.
$$

::: {.checkpoint-route}

You are ready to finish when you can read a backward zigzag arrow, distinguish
vineyard updates from diagram matching and explain what transport information
a vineyard module adds to visible vines.

:::
